title: The twisted trees
translation: Suketomo once took shelter from the rain in the gateway of Tōji temple. A group of disabled people were sitting there, their hands and feet twisted and bent back, every one of them misshapen in some strange way. "Each of them is a one-off," he thought. "Real curiosities. Well worth admiring." He stood and stared at them. But soon the fascination wore off, and they just looked ugly and depressing to him. "Nothing beats things that are plain and ordinary," he thought.

When he got home, it struck him: "All this time I've been into potted trees, looking for ones that are bent and twisted into strange shapes so I can enjoy looking at them. That's the same as admiring those people." It spoiled them for him, and he had every tree in every pot dug up and thrown away.
original: この{人|ひと}、{東寺|とうじ}の{門|もん}に{雨宿|あまやど}りせられたりけるに、かたは{者|もの}ども{集|あつま}り{居|ゐ}たるが、{手|て}も{足|あし}もねぢゆがみうち{反|かへ}りて、いづくも{不具|ふぐ}に{異様|いやう}なるを{見|み}て、
「とりどりに{類|たぐひ}なきくせ{者|もの}なり、{最|もつと}も{愛|あい}するに{足|た}れり。」と{思|おも}ひて、まもり{給|たま}ひけるほどに、
やがてその{興|きよう}つきて、{見|み}にくくいぶせく{覚|おぼ}えければ、「ただすなほに{珍|めづら}しからぬものには{如|し}かず。」と{思|おも}ひて、
{帰|かへ}りて{後|のち}、「この{間|あひだ}{植木|うゑき}を{好|この}みて、{異様|いやう}に{曲折|きよくせつ}あるを{求|もと}めて{目|め}を{喜|よろこ}ばしめつるは、かのかたは{者|もの}を{愛|あい}するなりけり。」と、{興|きよう}なく{覚|おぼ}えければ、{鉢|はち}に{栽|う}ゑられける{木|き}ども、みなほり{棄|す}てられにけり。

literal: This person, when he was sheltering from the rain at the gate of Tōji, saw that there were cripples gathered there, whose hands and feet were twisted, bent and turned back, everywhere deformed and strange,
and thinking, 'Each is an incomparable oddity; they are truly worth cherishing', he stared at them, and meanwhile
soon that interest ran out, and they seemed ugly and gloomy, so he thought, 'Nothing equals what is simply straight and not unusual', and

after he returned, thinking, 'Lately I have liked potted trees, and looked for ones with strange bends and twists to please my eyes: that was cherishing those cripples', he lost his pleasure in them, and the trees planted in pots were all dug up and thrown away.
That is surely as it should be.

notes.text: 'This person': Hino Suketomo again, from sections 152 and 153. The text uses respectful verbs for him all through (せられ, {給|たま}ひ, られ).
Tōji, the 'East Temple', in the south of Kyoto near the old main gate of the city. Emperor Saga gave it to Kūkai in the ninth century.
かたは: 'incomplete, deformed', an old word for physical disability that is offensive today. The section takes Suketomo's point of view, and the translation keeps what happens without the old word.
くせ{者|もの}: here 'a strange one, an oddity', from くせ, 'a quirk'. Modern {曲者|くせもの} means 'a suspicious character' or 'a tricky customer'.

notes.quote: ただすなほに珍しからぬものには如かず
notes.text: すなほ: 'straight, plain, natural'. Modern {素直|すなお} means 'honest, obedient'; the old word still meant 'straight' as well, which fits the twisted bodies and the bent trees. {如|し}かず: 'nothing equals', as in section 8.
{植木|うゑき}: here potted trees. Small trees grown in pots, the ancestor of bonsai, already appear in picture scrolls from around Kenkō's time, and Suketomo collects them here.
しむ: 'to make, to let'. 'To make my eyes glad'. つる is the attributive form of つ, a completed action.

notes.quote: さもありぬべきことなり
notes.text: Kenkō's own comment: 'that is quite understandable'. Compare section 36, which ends almost the same way.
